question: Which launch shape in the April planning pack gives us room to support an early cohort?
workload: The four documented startup cohorts in the ProfitCtl benchmark pack. Seats, demand, and support differ by scenario.
source_revision: ProfitCtl cb54ffea5781aed74a64c9d659494241f062328d; scenario input hashes below.
window: One modeled billing month. The comparison uses planning assumptions from April 2026.

alternatives.name: Free-heavy conservative launch
alternatives.cost: 30 active users. USD 700 revenue and USD 402.10 modeled monthly costs leave a 42.56% margin.
alternatives.quality: The plan supports self-serve evaluation. The modeled support reserve makes the early cohort miss its own margin threshold.

alternatives.name: Paid pilot
alternatives.cost: 15 active seats. USD 2,685 revenue and USD 407.05 modeled monthly costs leave an 84.84% margin.
alternatives.quality: The modeled concierge motion gives the team room to observe onboarding and corrections. Customer demand for this price is unknown.

alternatives.name: Tight free tier
alternatives.quality: A smaller free tier offers an alternative for evaluators. Their conversion rate is unmeasured.

alternatives.name: Workspace minimum
alternatives.quality: A workspace floor protects smaller accounts but adds pricing complexity.

evidence.finding: The four packaged scenarios passed through ProfitCtl compare. A failed covenant on the conservative scenario is a valid economic result (exit 1).
Routing, active-user mix, and onboarding labor need calibration. Each option represents a different cohort.

recommendation: Use the paid pilot for an initial pricing conversation and gather customer usage and support costs.
reversal_condition: Recompute if the real cohort cannot sustain the modeled price, support effort consumes the margin headroom, or a lower-touch free tier demonstrates stronger conversion.
missing: Representative paid invoices, accepted customer outcomes, net fees, actual seat mix, and human support time.
